description: Sole trader, partnership, LLP, Ltd and franchise compared, plus six start-up funding sources.
content_html:
Choosing a Legal Structure

When someone starts a business, one of the first decisions they face is how the business will be legally structured. This is not just administrative paperwork — the chosen structure determines who bears the financial risk, who controls the business, how profits are shared and how much it costs to set up. Getting it wrong can be costly later, so most entrepreneurs think carefully about structure from the start.

The most important concept that runs through all ownership types is unlimited liability. Under unlimited liability, the law treats the owner and the business as the same entity. If the business cannot pay its debts, the owner must pay them from their personal assets — including savings, a car or even a home. This is the greatest financial risk of certain ownership structures.

The opposite is limited liability. Under limited liability, the law treats the business as a separate legal entity from its owners. If the business fails, shareholders only lose what they put in — their personal possessions are safe. This protection makes limited liability structures attractive for any entrepreneur who is investing significant money or taking on meaningful risk.

Key Fact

Unlimited liability — a sole trader and general partners in a standard partnership are personally responsible for all business debts. Limited liability — shareholders in a private limited company (Ltd) and members of a limited liability partnership (LLP) can only lose what they invested. Examiners specifically test whether students know which structure gives which protection — writing “limited responsibility” instead of “limited liability” will cost marks.

The Four Ownership Types (Plus Franchise)

A sole trader is the simplest form of business ownership. There is no formal registration process beyond informing tax authorities. The owner makes all decisions, keeps all the profit after tax and has complete control. This suits independent tradespeople, personal trainers, freelancers and market traders who want flexibility and minimal administration.

The main disadvantages are unlimited liability — every business debt is a personal debt — and limited access to finance, since banks see sole traders as higher risk. If the owner becomes ill or is absent, the business may stop completely. There is also no one to share the workload or contribute complementary skills.

A partnership allows two or more people to go into business together, pooling their skills, experience and start-up capital. A furniture designer and a skilled carpenter, for example, might form a partnership that combines creative and craft expertise neither has alone. Partners share the workload, which can help a business grow faster than a sole trader could manage.

However, standard partners share unlimited liability. If one partner makes a poor business decision that creates a large debt, all partners are personally responsible — even if they had no involvement in that decision. A formal written partnership agreement, setting out each person’s role, decision-making rights and profit share, is strongly recommended to reduce disputes.

A limited liability partnership (LLP) is a variation that gives members the flexibility of a partnership while providing limited liability. This means members’ personal assets are protected if the business cannot pay its debts. LLPs are more common in professional services — law firms and accountancy practices, for example — but are an option available to any start-up that wants the combined skills of a partnership with the financial protection of limited liability.

A private limited company (Ltd) is legally separate from its owners. Shareholders invest in the company and have limited liability — they can only lose the money they put in. This structure requires formal registration with Companies House, and annual accounts are filed publicly. The administration is more complex and costly than a sole trader or partnership.

The advantages are significant: limited liability protects investors, capital can be raised by selling shares to trusted individuals, and the business continues to exist even if a founder leaves or dies. Shares in a private limited company cannot be sold on a stock exchange — they can only be transferred to buyers the existing shareholders approve. This keeps control within a trusted group, which many small business founders prefer.

A franchise is not a legal ownership structure in the same way as sole trader or Ltd — it describes a business operating model. A franchisee buys the right to trade under an established brand and follow a proven system. The advantage is significantly lower risk than starting from scratch: the brand is known, the product or service is tested, and the franchisor provides training and support.

The costs are real, however. The franchisee pays an upfront fee and ongoing royalties — typically a percentage of revenue — to the franchisor. They must follow the franchisor’s rules on pricing, branding and operations. This means the franchisee has far less independence than a sole trader or partner. For someone who wants to run their own business but values the security of a proven model, a franchise can be an attractive route into enterprise.

Key Fact

Sole trader: one owner, unlimited liability, full control, easy to set up. Partnership: shared skills and capital, unlimited liability, risk of disagreement. LLP: partnership flexibility, limited liability for members. Private limited company (Ltd): limited liability, separate legal entity, more administration. Franchise: proven model, lower risk, but less independence and ongoing royalty costs.

Six Sources of Start-Up Capital

Whatever structure a new business adopts, it needs money to get started. This money — called capital — can come from several sources. There are six sources to know.

  • Own savings — using personal savings avoids debt and interest costs. The entrepreneur keeps full control and all future profit. The risk is personal — if the business fails, the savings are lost.
  • Friends and family — money from people close to the entrepreneur can come as a gift (with no repayment obligation) or as an informal loan. This is often faster and easier to arrange than bank finance, but mixing money and personal relationships can create tension if the business struggles.
  • Loans — a bank or financial institution lends a fixed sum that must be repaid with interest over an agreed period. A loan provides a lump sum without giving away ownership of the business, but the obligation to make repayments continues even if sales are low. Note: the loan repayment itself is not classed as a business cost — only the interest on the loan is a cost.
  • Crowdfunding — the entrepreneur pitches the idea on an online platform and many individuals each contribute a small amount. In return, backers may receive an early product, a reward, or (in equity crowdfunding) a small share of the business. Crowdfunding can also generate publicity and test whether there is genuine demand before the product is made.
  • Grants — government bodies, local authorities and some other organisations offer grants to businesses that meet certain criteria, such as being in a specific industry or location. Unlike loans, grants do not have to be repaid, but they are competitive, often come with conditions on how the money is spent, and are not guaranteed.
  • Business angels — wealthy private investors who provide capital in exchange for a share of the business and often an active role as a mentor or advisor. A business angel brings not just money but contacts, experience and guidance. The entrepreneur gives up some ownership and must share future profits and decision-making authority.

Choosing the right source depends on how much capital is needed, how quickly it is needed, how much control the entrepreneur is willing to give up and what obligations come with the money.
exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Explain question about limited or unlimited liability, one fully developed point is worth more than two rushed ones. Use the structure: what the term means — what it means specifically for the business in the question — what the practical consequence is for the owner. A very common error is writing “limited responsibility” instead of “limited liability”, or claiming that a sole trader’s business assets are protected. Neither will earn marks. For 6-mark Analyse or 9-mark Discuss questions about ownership structure or finance sources, always embed a detail from the case-study scenario rather than writing a generic textbook definition — examiner reports consistently identify lack of application as the main barrier to reaching the Secure and Mastering tiers.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sole traders and standard partners have unlimited liability — personal assets are at risk. Shareholders in an Ltd and members of an LLP have limited liability — personal assets are protected. Using “limited responsibility” instead of “limited liability” is a mark-losing error.
  • The four ownership types are sole trader (full control, unlimited liability), partnership (shared skills, unlimited liability), LLP (partnership flexibility plus limited liability) and private limited company (limited liability, separate legal entity). A franchise is a different kind of start-up model: lower risk but less independence and ongoing royalty costs.
  • The six sources of start-up capital are: own savings, friends and family (gift or loan), loans (interest is a cost; repayment is not), crowdfunding, grants and business angels. Each has trade-offs between cost, control and obligation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following business structures gives its owners limited liability?
A) Sole trader
B) Standard partnership
C) Private limited company (Ltd)
D) A business with one owner and no formal registration
State two disadvantages of operating as a sole trader.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each correct disadvantage, up to 2 marks:
• Unlimited liability — personal assets (home, savings) can be seized if the business cannot pay its debts [1 mark]
• Difficult to raise large amounts of finance, as banks see sole traders as higher risk [1 mark]
• The business depends entirely on the owner — illness or absence can stop it functioning [1 mark]
• All decisions rest with one person — no one to share workload or complementary skills [1 mark]
[Any two of the above for 2 marks; no further development required for Describe questions at 1 mark per point]

practice_questions.text: Outline one difference between a standard partnership and a limited liability partnership (LLP).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for a point with development:
• In a standard partnership, all partners have unlimited liability and personal assets can be claimed to pay business debts (1 mark); in an LLP, members have limited liability, so personal assets are protected if the business cannot pay what it owes (1 mark).
[1 mark for identifying the liability difference; 2 marks for explaining the implication for personal assets]

practice_questions.text:
Perch & Frame is a small picture-framing business in Brighton run by Yasmin. She currently operates as a sole trader. A friend has offered to invest £15,000 in exchange for a 30% share of the business. Yasmin is worried about personal financial risk as the business grows.

Explain two reasons why Yasmin might consider forming a private limited company.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per point (statement plus development), maximum 4 marks:
• Limited liability would protect Yasmin's personal assets (1 mark) — as a shareholder in an Ltd, she could only lose her investment if Perch & Frame failed, meaning her home and savings would be safe, which directly addresses her concern about personal financial risk as the business grows (1 mark).
• Bringing in the investor as a shareholder creates a formal legal arrangement (1 mark) — it clearly defines the investor's 30% ownership stake and Yasmin's 70% majority, giving both parties legal clarity and preventing future disputes about control or profit sharing (1 mark).
[Credit any two valid, developed reasons linked to the scenario]

practice_questions.text:
Sable & Fern is a new zero-waste cleaning products brand founded by two friends, Priya and Joel, in Manchester. They are deciding how to fund the first production run.

Priya wants to use a crowdfunding platform. Joel wants to apply for a business grant.

Analyse the benefits and drawbacks of each funding option for Sable & Fern.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Both crowdfunding and grants are analysed with developed points on at least one benefit and one drawback of each. Contextual details (zero-waste brand, two founders, first production run) are embedded throughout rather than added as a label. The response shows analytical connections between the funding type and the specific situation Sable & Fern faces.

Secure (3-4 marks): Both options are addressed with some analytical development. At least one benefit and one drawback across the two options are developed. Some use of context.

Developing (2 marks): One or both options are described with limited analytical development. Context from the scenario is largely absent.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic and partly correct description of one funding option with no analytical development.

practice_questions.text:
Remy has decided to start a business. He is considering two options:
Option A: Set up as a sole trader selling handmade candles online.
Option B: Buy a cleaning franchise with an established UK brand.

Justify which option you would recommend for Remy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A clear recommendation is made and justified with developed reasoning addressing the key trade-offs between control and risk (sole trader: full independence, unlimited liability, no proven model; franchise: lower risk, proven brand, but ongoing royalty costs and loss of independence). The recommendation is consistent and the conclusion adds a new evaluative point not already made in the body.

Secure (3-4 marks): A recommendation is made with clear reasoning and some awareness of trade-offs. The response is more developed than a simple list of pros and cons.

Developing (2 marks): A preference is stated with brief and partly developed reasoning. Trade-offs are described but not fully analysed.

Emerging (1 mark): A preference is stated with limited or no reasoned justification.

knowledge_checks.q: What does 'unlimited liability' mean for a sole trader?
options: The business can borrow unlimited funds from a bank
The owner's personal assets can be used to pay business debts
The owner is not responsible for any debts incurred by employees
The owner keeps all profits without paying tax

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six sources of start-up capital covered in this lesson?
A private limited company is legally _____ from its owners, meaning shareholders have limited liability.
In a franchise arrangement, the franchisee pays ongoing _____ to the franchisor — a percentage of revenue — in addition to the upfront fee.
Match each business structure to its key characteristic:
right: Owned by one person with unlimited liability and full control
Members have the flexibility of a partnership but with personal asset protection
A separate legal entity with limited liability for shareholders; shares sold only by agreement

flashcard_questions.a: The owner is personally responsible for all business debts; creditors can claim personal assets.
Owners can only lose the money they invested; personal assets are protected from business debts.

flashcard_questions.q: Which ownership structures carry unlimited liability?

flashcard_questions.a: A business owned and run by one person who keeps all profits but has unlimited liability.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a limited liability partnership (LLP)?
flashcard_questions.a: A partnership structure where members have personal asset protection alongside partnership flexibility.

flashcard_questions.q: What makes a private limited company (Ltd) different from a sole trader on liability?
flashcard_questions.a: Ltd shareholders have limited liability; a sole trader has unlimited liability.

flashcard_questions.q: In a franchise, what ongoing payment does the franchisee make to the franchisor?
Give one advantage of buying a franchise over starting from scratch.
flashcard_questions.a: Lower risk — the brand is established and the business model is proven.

flashcard_questions.q: Can friends and family finance be a gift or a loan?
flashcard_questions.a: Both — the spec confirms it can be either a gift or an informal loan.

flashcard_questions.q: When a business takes a loan, what is classed as a business cost?
flashcard_questions.a: The interest on the loan — not the repayment of the loan itself.
Raising capital from many small contributions via an online platform, often in exchange for rewards.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a business angel typically receive in exchange for their investment?
Why might a sole trader convert to a private limited company as the business grows?
flashcard_questions.a: To gain limited liability and protect personal assets as financial risk increases.

glossary_terms.definition: Where owners are personally responsible for all business debts; creditors can pursue the owner's personal savings, home and possessions to recover what is owed.
Where owners can only lose the money they have invested in the business; personal assets are protected if the business cannot pay its debts.
A business owned and run by a single person who keeps all the profits but has unlimited liability for all business debts.
A business owned by two or more people who share profits, decision-making and, in a standard partnership, unlimited liability for business debts.
A business structure where members have the benefits of partnership but also enjoy limited liability, protecting personal assets from business debts.
A business incorporated as a separate legal entity from its owners, where shareholders have limited liability and shares can only be sold to people the shareholders agree to.
An arrangement where a franchisee pays to operate under an established brand and use the franchisor's proven business systems, in exchange for an upfront fee and ongoing royalties.
